logs: verification capped at 22 of 61 blocker/major findings

lenses.summary: First-contact usability audit of Holdfast, performed as a real newbie journey: read README.md only, built a scratch JVM project (/tmp/holdfast-uxtest, left in place), pasted the quick-start, then added holdfast-coroutines — 5 gradle invocations total. Empirical log: (1) the artifact does not exist on Maven Central despite the badge and install instructions (curl 404 on the whole com.vynatix group); mavenLocal stand-in used, where holdfast-testing/hallmark artifacts are also missing. (2) Faithful README paste → 18 compile errors: zero imports shown (the top-level infix `effect` import is unguessable) plus an undefined `handle()` placeholder. (3) After 3 imports + 1 placeholder fix, the sample ran and the atomic-rollback promise verified perfectly — but the deliberately failing transaction produced zero output: errors are silently swallowed into an ignorable TransactionResult with no Result-style helpers. (4) Step two (coroutines) compiled first try, but only because core leaks kotlinx-coroutines api-scoped — directly contradicting three doc claims of 'no coroutines in core'; the module README documents neither suspendAction (its headline feature) nor matches current class names. (5) A probe proved the worst footgun: writing `store { ... }` instead of `store action { ... }` compiles silently and commits each write separately, with observers firing between writes — the exact non-atomicity the library exists to prevent. Doc rot from an unfinished three-generation rename (vault → holdfast → Store) is pervasive: the advertised `holdfastTest { }` API is actually named `vaultTest`, holdfast-testing and holdfast-hallmark have no README at all, three module READMEs use nonexistent *Holdfast classes, and the pitfalls table quotes error messages that don't exist in code. Verdict: the core engineering and its transactional value proposition are strong and verifiably honest at runtime, but distribution (blocker), rename-rotted docs, and two silent-failure footguns (invoke-vs-action, swallowed errors) would stop or burn most adopters today. 16 findings: 2 blockers, 6 major, 6 minor, 2 polish; 9 strengths."}
strengths: The core transactional promise is real and verified: in the empirical run, a throwing action rolled back atomically — observers never fired for the staged write and the value was untouched. No StateFlow/Orbit/MVIKotlin equivalent gives multi-cell atomic commit with rollback; this is a genuine niche.

JVM-only consumption of the KMP artifact worked first try: a plain kotlin("jvm") project resolved com.vynatix:holdfast:0.1.0 from a Maven repo with zero platform-suffix or metadata gymnastics — better than many KMP libraries at this maturity stage.

suspendAction worked exactly as documented on first attempt, including the subtle part: a 10ms suspend inside the transaction never leaked the staged value into a concurrently collecting asFlow — the flow saw only initial value then committed value, in order. The concurrency contract KDoc (SuspendAction.kt:20-46) covering cancellation-rollback, NonCancellable commit fanout, and middleware ordering is among the most precise I've seen in a 0.x library.
errors-as-values design (action never throws, Transaction.kt:361-372) is a defensible, predictable choice — it just needs Result-style helpers and louder docs (see findings).

The Positioning section (holdfast/README.md:150-174) honestly tells users when NOT to use the library ('If your state is one value, use StateFlow and skip this library') and positions accurately against Redux/MVI/Molecule — rare candor that builds trust.

Module layering matches ecosystem best practice: core / coroutines / compose / testing split with api(project(":holdfast")) (holdfast-coroutines/build.gradle.kts:55) mirrors what Orbit and MVIKotlin adopters expect, and the compose module deliberately brings only compose.runtime.

Consumer-hygiene infrastructure is in place: binary-compatibility validator (apiCheck), published sources jars, Dokka, and .git-blame-ignore-revs maintenance — signals a maintainer who takes API stability seriously even at 0.x.

GUIDE.md's structure (decision charts, visibility model, pitfalls table, seven-primitives taxonomy, workflow diagram) is the right shape for teaching a transactional mental model that has no ecosystem precedent — the content just needs to catch up to the rename (see findings).
Effects firing immediately with the current value on subscribe matches StateFlow expectations and is correctly documented in the quick-start comment (// count=0) — verified empirically.

lenses.summary: Usability review of Holdfast core API surface (lens: ergonomics + naming), based on source reading of all core files, the JVM ABI dump, and 6 compile/runtime probes against the built holdfast-jvm-0.1.0.jar. The library's transactional core is a real differentiator with excellent KDoc, but four empirically-verified footguns cluster around one theme: failures are too quiet. (1) `action` swallows every Throwable into an ignorable TransactionResult with zero unwrap affordances anywhere in the ecosystem (blocker). (2) The flagship self-type `Store<Self : Store<Self>>` does NOT enforce self-anchoring — `class Foo : Store<Bar>()` compiles silently and degrades to a runtime CCE swallowed into that same ignorable result; the README's central type-safety claim is false. (3) Standalone `update` is a non-atomic RMW (measured: 5049 of 10000 concurrent increments survive) where StateFlow.update — the audience's muscle memory — is an atomic CAS. (4) `store { }` vs `store action { }` differ by one token but flip atomicity/rollback/error capture (verified: mid-block throw leaves earlier mutates committed). Additional majors: lazy delegate registration makes snapshot()/restore() silently empty/failing on un-touched stores; distinct=false inverts StateFlow's dedup contract (verified re-fires); vault/store/holdfast terminology drift persists into permanent public symbols (bindVault, owningVault); and several genuinely ungated internals (MutableState constructor, StoreLock, Transaction.commit) are callable from app code without opt-in (verified). Most fixes are cheap and the 0.x window makes them feasible now: add getOrThrow/onError to TransactionResult, use provideDelegate for eager state registration, wrap standalone update's read in its synthesized action, flip or rename distinct, and finish the vault→store rename."
strengths: Transactional rollback semantics are genuinely novel vs the StateFlow/MVI ecosystem and crisply specified: buffered writes, read-your-own-writes on the owner thread, throw-discards-everything, savepoint nesting (Store.kt:331-352, Transaction.kt:7-19). Nothing in Orbit/MVIKotlin/Redux-Kotlin gives multi-property atomic commit with rollback.

Cross-store `atomic(v1, v2) {}` with deadlock-safe global lock ordering via lockOrderKey (Atomic.kt:10-66) is a capability competitors simply don't have; the KDoc honestly lists 1.1 limitations (non-suspending body, single-threaded body).

Foreign-state ownership check fails fast with O(1) identity comparison (Store.kt:565-570) instead of silently corrupting another store — the GUIDE explicitly motivates this against the casts-succeed-bug-ships failure mode (GUIDE.md:51).

The best error messages teach the fix: EventfulSupport.emit before bindVault tells you exactly what to call and where (EventfulSupport.kt:106-114); emit outside an action explains WHY events must be transactional (EventfulStore.kt:89-96); removeState with pending writes says 'commit or rollback first' (Store.kt:629).

State-vs-event back-pressure split is better articulated than most MVI libraries: State.asFlow() = DROP_OLDEST (recoverable), Eventful.events = SUSPEND (lossless), with the rationale in user-facing KDoc (Eventful.kt:6-26) and a documented commit-phase ordering contract — observers, then bridges, then events (EventfulStore.kt:30-37).

Naming symmetry across modules is excellent: action/suspendAction, atomic/suspendAtomic, derived/suspendDerived, asFlow/asStateFlow, bridge/suspendingBridge (holdfast-coroutines api dump) — learn the core once, the suspend surface is predictable.

@StoreInternalApi with ERROR-level @RequiresOptIn (StoreInternalApi.kt) is the correct mechanism for cross-module internals — misuse is a compile error, not a convention; and the message invites filing an issue rather than opting in.
@DslMarker on the store DSL (StoreActionDsl.kt) prevents nested-action receiver leakage — cross-store references inside nested actions must be explicit, which Redux-style DSLs frequently get wrong.

computed() vs derived() is a well-drawn pull-vs-push distinction with honest trade-off documentation (cost multiplication in derived chains, recompute thread) right in the KDoc (Derived.kt:8-23, 42-46).

Transformer.then composition documents its round-trip law and asymmetric-transformer guarantee (rollback never re-runs set) (Contract.kt:54-93) — the snapshot/restore raw-value design (Snapshot.kt:8-17) correctly avoids double-encrypting ciphertext.

binary-compatibility API dumps are maintained per-module (holdfast/api/jvm/holdfast.api), and KDoc coverage on the public surface is near-total, including concurrency contracts (volatile semantics, lock ordering) that most libraries leave undocumented.
Scope resolution chain (per-call > subclass override > bindToScope > process default) is fully specified including the lazy-init trap warning for singleton stores (Store.kt:70-99).

lenses.summary: Error-experience lens on Holdfast core + coroutines. The library's runtime guards are unusually strong for the category (foreign-state ownership check, transactional emit gating, settable-once defaultScope, stale-transaction guards, disposed checks — most with tests asserting messages), but three systemic issues undercut them: (1) `action` never throws, returns TransactionResult with no must-use enforcement, so every guard's error can be silently discarded in the idiomatic fire-and-forget call style — this converts the foreign-state check, Transformer validation, restore() failures, and disposed-store errors (under suspendAction) into silent no-ops; (2) two silent-misbehavior holes remain: observer exceptions are swallowed by default (uncaughtObserverHandler is null and nearly undocumented) and emit() lacks the ownership check mutate has, so a racy off-action emit silently stages onto a foreign transaction; plus commit-fanout exceptions (transformer.get / bridge.publish) yield PARTIAL commits despite the all-or-nothing promise; (3) doc accuracy on the error paths is poor exactly where users will be debugging: GUIDE 9.8's nested-action error-propagation claims are the opposite of the implementation (contradicted by the library's own test), the pitfalls table quotes an error string that exists nowhere in the code, the middleware-ordering paragraph inverts the real order, and dispose()/defaultScope/uncaughtObserverHandler have no narrative docs at all. Exception types are generic IllegalStateException nearly everywhere (only TransactionException is custom), forcing message-string matching for programmatic handling. Messages themselves range from exemplary (emit-outside-action explains the rationale) to anemic ('store disposed' — no store identity, no disposal site; 'State must be created by this Store instance' — no property or store names despite both being available)."
strengths: Foreign-state ownership is actually checked at runtime (Store.kt:561-570, O(1) identity check via owningVault) — StateFlow/MVI ecosystems have no equivalent guard; passing the wrong flow into the wrong reducer silently corrupts state. Here it deterministically errors, and @StoreActionDsl (Store.kt:47, StoreActionDsl marker) additionally blocks the nested-receiver variant at COMPILE time.

The emit-outside-action error message is exemplary error design: it names the violated rule AND its rationale — 'emit(event) called outside of an action / suspendAction. Events must be staged inside a transaction so rollback can discard them.' (EventfulStore.kt:91-94). EventfulSupport's bind errors are equally instructive ('The hosting Store must call support.bindVault(this) in its init block.', EventfulSupport.kt:106-109).

Stale-Transaction misuse is defended: mutating via a committed/rolled-back transaction throws 'Cannot mutate state on a Committed transaction' (Store.kt:546-549) instead of silently dropping the write, and commit/rollback are idempotent no-ops on finalized transactions (Transaction.kt:165-171, 289-291) — a thoughtful 'can't replay side effects' contract.

removeState/clearStates refuse to drop states with pending writes, with an actionable message: 'Cannot remove state 'x' with pending writes in an active transaction; commit or rollback first' (Store.kt:623-631).

Store.defaultScope is CAS-guarded settable-once with a clear message (Store.kt:711-717) — vs the silent last-write-wins global config most libraries ship; prevents two modules fighting over the process scope without noticing.

TransactionResult is a sealed interface with Error carrying BOTH the exception and the transaction (Transaction.kt:361-371), enabling exhaustive `when` and post-mortem inspection — richer than Redux/MVI dispatch which typically returns Unit and routes errors to a side channel.

Per-observer exception isolation: one throwing observer cannot starve the rest of the fanout (MutableState.kt:167-175 catches per observer inside the loop), and initial-fire exceptions deliberately propagate to the subscriber (MutableState.kt:198-199, rationale documented at Store.kt:217-221) so subscribe-time bugs are loud.

Disposed-store behavior is contract-tested including message content (StoreDisposeTest.kt asserts 'disposed' appears in the message for action/mutate/update/effect), and dispose() is idempotent by CAS (Store.kt:136-140).

@StoreInternalApi at RequiresOptIn.Level.ERROR with a message that tells app developers to file an issue instead of opting in (StoreInternalApi.kt:13-18) — internal hooks are a compile error to touch casually.

Lifecycle-managed adapters make the leak-free path the easy path: compose collectAsState/rememberDisposable auto-dispose on leaving composition (ComposeBindings.kt:33-63), asFlow disposes its observer when collection cancels (StateFlows.kt:52-57).

GUIDE.md ships a Common Pitfalls symptom→cause→fix table (GUIDE.md:995-1006) and copy-pasteable testing patterns including cross-store rejection and rollback invisibility (GUIDE.md:913-991) — the right documentation genre for error experience, even where individual entries are stale.

lenses.summary: Usability review of Holdfast's concurrency/scoping model. The core finding is a split between excellent in-source KDoc and a user-facing doc layer (GUIDE.md, module READMEs) that never mentions scopes, bindToScope, defaultScope, or dispose, and is stale against the current API. One blocker: the K2 context(CoroutineScope) overload pairs on asStateFlow and the bridge factories silently capture any ambient coroutine receiver (launch/runBlocking/LaunchedEffect bodies), producing silently-dead StateFlows — and the KDoc's resolution claim is contradicted by the project's own test comments. Major findings: observers run on the committing thread under the transaction lock while contenders busy-spin (with GUIDE.md:868 claiming the opposite); blocking action{} nested in or concurrent with suspendAction degenerates to an undetectable infinite spin (guaranteed freeze on wasmJs); defaultScope's settable-once contract breaks user test suites with no help from holdfast-testing; and the coroutines README/GUIDE document a removed API and an outdated signature. Strengths: the scope chain and dispose asymmetry are precisely specified in KDoc, defaults are safe and non-leaking, sync/async mutual exclusion is automatic, commit fanout is cancellation-proof, and behavior-change/platform-limit messaging is unusually honest where present.
strengths: The 4-level scope resolution chain is explicitly enumerated with rationale at its definition site (Store.kt:71-84), including the subtle 'override beats bound' precedence and the 'use a getter, not a val initializer' singleton trap — most StateFlow/MVI libraries leave scope plumbing entirely implicit.

Zero-config defaults are safe: asStateFlow() defaults to SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed + the store-resolved scope (StateFlows.kt:90-93), so a user with no scope setup gets a working, non-leaking StateFlow; the lazy process default (Store.kt:688-690) means nothing crashes when nothing is configured.

defaultScope fails fast and loud on double-assignment with an explicit message (Store.kt:711-717) instead of silent last-writer-wins — the failure mode is annoying in tests but never produces mystery behavior.

Blocking action{} and suspendAction{} are mutually exclusive by default via the lazily-installed serializer (Store.kt:359-365, AsyncSerializer.kt:47-57) — no 'two concurrency worlds' split-brain where sync and async mutations interleave, a real gap in several MVI libraries.

suspendAction commits under NonCancellable (SuspendAction.kt:144-167) so cancellation can never leave observers/bridges half-notified, and cancellation-vs-error semantics (rollback + rethrow CE) are explicitly specified in the KDoc contract (SuspendAction.kt:32-36).

Behavior-change documentation is exemplary where it exists: StateFlows.kt:31-39 documents the 1.x→2.0 asFlow delivery-contract change ('you may miss intermediate values; you will always see the latest'), names the old failure mode, and points to the right tool (events SharedFlow) for lossless delivery — including stating which thread emissions occur on.

Platform-limit error messages are actionable: the wasmJs runBlocking actual throws with the cause and a concrete workaround in the message (RunBlocking.kt wasmJs:4-8), rather than a generic UnsupportedOperationException.

dispose() contract is precise and idempotent with the scope-asymmetry called out exactly where a reader needs it (Store.kt:123-134), and foreign-state ownership is checked at mutate time with an immediate throw (Store.kt:565-570) instead of silent cross-store corruption.

GUIDE §10 ships a real lock table and a global lock-ordering statement (GUIDE.md:860-880) — even with one inaccurate row, publishing the internal lock order for extension authors is more concurrency transparency than Orbit/MVIKotlin docs attempt.
suspendDerived documents its race semantics honestly ('later result wins', no coalescing, debounce-upstream advice) and its full cancellation matrix (SuspendDerived.kt:27-44) instead of hand-waving.

lenses.summary: Documentation accuracy audit of Holdfast (6 KMP modules) cross-checking README.md, holdfast/README.md, holdfast/GUIDE.md (1,692 lines), module READMEs, and changelogs against the checked-in .api dumps and source. Verdict: the core-library quick-start docs are accurate and unusually well-crafted (pedagogical GUIDE, written concurrency model, honest 0.x framing), but everything at the edges is untrustworthy. One adoption blocker: the install instructions, Maven Central badge, and changelog all claim com.vynatix:holdfast:0.1.0 is on Maven Central — live checks return 404/zero results, so a new user's first Gradle sync fails. The Holdfast↔Store↔Vault rename was completed mechanically in core but leaked everywhere else: the documented test entry point `holdfastTest{}` is actually `vaultTest` (with `bindVault`, `owningVault`, and a `CountVault` KDoc sample still in the public surface), four docs still use CounterHoldfast/AccountHoldfast/UserHoldfast class names, and GUIDE §14.11 plus the hallmark-coroutines README still use pre-rename `com.vynatix:validation*` module coordinates. Five doc claims directly contradict code: 'no coroutines dependency in core' (build has api(kotlinx-coroutines-core); Store.scope/EventfulStore are public), same-value-commit dedup described as default (requires opt-in distinct=true), middleware ordering in §4.6 (inverted vs source), `transaction(on=store)` presented as a core primitive (it's a test-only open-transaction utility in holdfast-testing), and `asEagerStateFlow` documented though removed. Eight `../MIGRATING.md` links and a KONFORM-MIGRATION link are dead. Coverage gaps: lifecycle/scope/dispose and the Eventful events system are documented only inside the 'internal-only history' changelog; holdfast-testing and holdfast-hallmark have no README; holdfast-coroutines README documents 4 of ~10 features; the only Compose example doesn't compile (variable-shadowing bug); GUIDE §14 is organized around internal version numbers (1.0/1.1/2.0) no published artifact ever carried. Fix priority: (1) publish or de-claim Maven Central, (2) finish the rename in the public API (vaultTest/bindVault/owningVault) and docs, (3) reconcile the five behavior contradictions, (4) write the lifecycle + testing + module-chooser docs."
strengths: The day-one quick-start path is accurate: every identifier in README.md:15-39 and holdfast/README.md:17-46 and GUIDE §3 (state/action/mutate/update/effect/bridge/invoke, TransactionResult.Success/Error fields) exists with matching infix forms (verified against holdfast/api/jvm/holdfast.api and Store.kt:354,488,500,520,534, Effect.kt:26). Core samples copy-paste-compile, which is better than most 0.x libraries manage.

GUIDE.md's pedagogy is genuinely above ecosystem standard: a real TOC, a 30-second pitch, ASCII transaction-lifecycle and status-machine diagrams (§5), a who-sees-what-when visibility table (§6), decision charts (§7), and a pitfalls table (§12) that maps actual exception strings ('Failed to record state change', 'Cannot mutate state on a Committed transaction') to causes and fixes — Orbit/MVIKotlin/Redux-style docs rarely document failure-mode UX at all.

An explicit, written concurrency model (GUIDE §10: per-store reentrant lock, global lock ordering, thread confinement, an honest 'what is NOT thread-safe' list; holdfast/README.md:126-137) — this is the single most under-documented area in competing state libraries and Holdfast leads with it.

Binary-compatibility .api dumps are checked in for all six modules and wired to :apiCheck (documented in holdfast/README.md:192) — adopters can ground-truth the docs against a machine-checked surface, and this audit could too.

Honest framing where it counts: 0.x 'pin exact versions' stability warnings in both READMEs, XorCipher explicitly labeled 'NOT production-grade' in three places, and the changelog cleanly quarantines pre-rename history as 'internal-only design archive' with reading order guidance.

The testing module's design is a real differentiator: vaultTest's teardown fails the test on unconsumed TransactionResult.Error (StoreTest.kt:21-27) — a thoughtful guard against the 'action never throws' API silently swallowing failures — plus timeline events, matcher DSLs, deterministic concurrency helpers (Barrier, eventually, openTransaction) and bridge fakes (FailingBridge, LatchedBridge, RecordingBridge). It just needs documentation.

TransactionResult-as-value error handling (action never throws; sealed Success/Error with the body's return value flowing into Success<R>) is consistently presented across all docs and matches the implementation — a clear, teachable contract vs the try/catch soup of imperative stores.
Positioning section (holdfast/README.md:150-174) honestly tells users when NOT to use the library ('If your state is one value, use StateFlow and skip this library') — rare candor that builds trust.

lenses.summary: The holdfast-testing harness is the most ambitious part of the library and much of it is genuinely best-in-class: the unconsumed-error teardown guard with its actionable failure message, automatic leak cleanup (open transactions, barriers, awaiting channels), race-free awaiting{} replay semantics, purpose-built bridge fakes, and self-contained matchers with concrete failure text all exceed what StateFlow/Turbine/Orbit/MVIKotlin users have today. But the adoption funnel is broken at the very first step: both READMEs document a `holdfastTest { }` entry point that does not exist (the real function is `vaultTest`, named after an abandoned brand and invisible to Store*/Holdfast IDE searches), the module has no README, and GUIDE.md's testing chapter never mentions the harness. Past that, three silent traps will bite most users: (1) core's member `Store.action` shadows the scope's auto-tracking `action {}`, so the natural `v.action {}` call records nothing and — critically — its errors bypass the pending-error guard, an inconsistency the harness's own tests work around with commented `v.read { }` warm-ups; (2) `suspendAction` produces zero timeline events by v1 contract, so async tests see empty timelines with failure messages that never hint why; (3) matcher categories that v1 can never record (user middleware, late-attached bridges) make `shouldNotFire` permanently green and `middleware<M>()` without a property access registers no predicate at all. Dependency hygiene also needs work: kotest-assertions is api-exposed yet unused in any line of code, and hallmark rides along for one 27-line matcher. The fixes are mostly cheap (rename + doc sweep, drop kotest, fail-loud on unrecordable predicates, synthesize suspendAction events); the underlying architecture is sound and worth them.
strengths: The pending-error guard is a genuinely novel safety net the StateFlow/Orbit/MVIKotlin ecosystem lacks: every TransactionResult.Error from a tracked handle must be asserted on or explicitly discarded, and the teardown message is exemplary — StoreTestScope.kt:188-199 produces 'vaultTest body finished with N unconsumed TransactionResult.Error value(s):' followed by per-error lines '[#1] handle=CounterStore@1a2b IllegalStateException "oops" (txn \'...\')' and the exact remediation: 'Call .shouldBeError / .shouldBeSuccess / .shouldRollbackWith on each, or use handle.consumeAllPendingErrors() to opt out.' It is also correctly suppressed when the body already threw (StoreTest.kt:38-46) so the root cause is what the runner reports.

Teardown leak-proofing is comprehensive and ordered (StoreTestScope.kt:155-171): forgotten barriers are cancelled, suspended awaiting{} channels are closed, leaked OpenTransactions are auto-rolled-back so pending writes never bleed into the next test, recorders detach. Competing harnesses (Turbine 'unconsumed events' aside) rarely clean up this much user error automatically.

Failure messages across the matcher set are concrete and self-describing: shouldFire lists each unmatched predicate by human description ('transaction \'foo\' committed'), shouldFireInExactOrder names the index and the actual event class it found instead (TimelineMatcherRunner.kt:118-127), StateMatchers prints per-property 'name: expected=X actual=Y' lines, and misuse errors are instructional — e.g. list-receiver emitted() throws 'requires a store context. Use StoreHandle... instead' (TimelineMatcher.kt:182-188) and bridge() on an unwrappable bridge says 'Attach it BEFORE track(v) so the recorder can wrap it, or use a RecordingBridge / LatchedBridge' (StoreHandle.kt:229-233).

awaiting{} has race-free semantics most hand-rolled flow tests get wrong: snapshot-and-subscribe runs atomically under the recorder lock (Recorder.kt:151-159), so an event is seen exactly once via replay or live channel — eliminating the missed-event-before-collect race familiar from StateFlow testing. Its timeout error includes a recent-event tail for diagnosis.

Virtual-time integration is coherent: eventually{} and awaiting{} participate in the TestScheduler so polling 'over 1 second' completes in near-zero wall time, while parallel{} deliberately uses real Dispatchers.Default with a clearly documented deadlock rationale (Parallel.kt:14-22) — an unusually honest treatment of the virtual-time/lock interaction.

The bridge test kit (FakeKvStore with defensive snapshots, RecordingBridge, LatchedBridge with awaitPublishAttempt, FailingBridge with Publish/Observe/Both failure modes, BridgeView.receiving for synthesizing inbound updates) is purpose-built fake infrastructure that Redux/MVI testing ecosystems simply do not ship — users normally have to write all of this themselves.

track() idempotency by reference identity means explicit track(v) and implicit v.read{} can never fork into two handles with divergent timelines (HandleRegistry via StoreTestScope.kt:72-75) — a forgiving design for mixed styles.

KDoc honesty about v1 limits is far above ecosystem norm: the Recorder documents its hook strategy and every known gap (commit-time errors, unwrapped user middleware, suspendAction) with v2 intent (Recorder.kt:57-72), and LatchedBridge documents exactly why it deviates from spec and what stays stable (LatchedBridge.kt:14-33). The matchers being hand-rolled with zero runtime assertion-library dependency (despite the build file suggesting otherwise) means the harness works identically for kotest and non-kotest users.
Capture modes (All / None / RingBuffer) give explicit overhead control for long-running stress tests (Capture.kt), something no comparable state-testing DSL offers.

lenses.summary: Holdfast's conceptual pitch is unusually honest and its GUIDE depth (decision charts, visibility tables, pitfalls, lock ordering) beats most of the Kotlin state-management ecosystem — but the onboarding funnel is broken at the very first step and frayed by an unfinished triple rename. Blockers: the README's install block points at Maven Central where com.vynatix has zero artifacts (badge, install snippet, and CHANGELOG all claim publication), and the advertised testing entry point `holdfastTest { }` doesn't exist (real name: `vaultTest`). Major systemic issues cluster into three themes: (1) brand archaeology — Vault-era names survive in public API (bindVault, owningVault), KDoc samples (CounterVault/MyVault), module READMEs (CounterHoldfast), and the GUIDE organizes features under internal version numbers (1.1/2.0/0.3.0) and stale module names (:validation) that no consumer can map to the shipped 0.1.0; (2) undocumented load-bearing API — Store.dispose()/scope/bindToScope and the entire Eventful events system (the MVI one-shot-events answer) are public core API absent from README and GUIDE, leaving the ViewModel/DI/lifecycle integration story (who calls dispose?) unanswerable from docs, with no migration guide from StateFlow/MVI and no Hilt/Koin content; (3) accuracy drift that hits trust — 'no coroutines in core' is contradicted by api(kotlinx-coroutines-core), same-value dedup is documented as default in two GUIDE sections but is opt-in (distinct=false) in code, wasmJs is headlined as supported while its tests are build-disabled and FileSystemKvStore throws on construction, snapshot/restore is marketed without disclosing it cannot serve Android process death (internal constructor, unreadable values), and action/observer failures are silent by default. Genuine strengths worth preserving: the 'skip this library if your state is one value' candor, the sealed TransactionResult error channel, foreign-store rejection, compose.runtime-only layering, ABI-checked modules, and a live companion demo repo. Most fixes are documentation sweeps plus a handful of pre-1.0 renames — cheap now, expensive after 1.0."
strengths: Honest 'you do not need this if' positioning, rare in the ecosystem: holdfast/README.md:154-158 explicitly says 'If your state is one value, use StateFlow and skip this library', and the Redux/Molecule/Saga comparisons concede their advantages (serializable-action replay) rather than strawmanning them.

Honest stability and security posture: 0.x may-break-anytime with pin-exact-version advice stated in three places (README.md:84-87, holdfast/README.md:182-185, CHANGELOG.md:6-7); XorCipher is loudly marked 'NOT production-grade' with concrete javax.crypto/CryptoKit guidance (GUIDE.md:1207-1210); the wasm FileSystemKvStore actual fails fast with an actionable message naming alternatives (FileSystemKvStore.wasmJs.kt:10-14).

Documentation depth far above the Kotlin-library norm: GUIDE.md ships decision charts (§7), a who-sees-what-when visibility table (§6), a transaction lifecycle diagram (§5), lock-ordering documentation (§10.2), a symptom-first pitfalls table (§12), and copy-paste testing patterns (§11). The quickstart genuinely is complete day-one usage in ~20 lines (GUIDE.md:127-161).

The CRTP `Store<Self>` pattern — usually an adoption scare — is explained with its rationale up front ('exists so the inside of a transaction has access to your state class's properties without casting', holdfast/README.md:66-69), and the property-delegate declaration style (`val count by state { 0 }`) pattern-matches Compose conventions for instant familiarity.

`action` returning a sealed `TransactionResult<R>` with the body's value in Success (Store.kt:332-354) gives an explicit, exhaustive error channel that MVI users will recognize, and rollback semantics (observers never fire, bridges never publish, savepoint merging for nested actions) are precisely specified and consistently implemented.

Genuine engineering-hygiene trust signals: per-module ABI dumps with apiCheck, detekt/ktlint, dokka, and a real companion demo repo (github.com/vynatix/banking-demo, verified live) claimed to exercise every public API with 186 feature-coverage tests.

Foreign-store mutation is rejected at runtime with an O(1) ownership check instead of silently corrupting state (Store.kt:561-570) — a class of bug StateFlow/Redux setups ship to production; the docs even include a test pattern for it (GUIDE.md:961-972).

Module layering matches ecosystem expectations: core / -coroutines / -compose / -testing split, with holdfast-compose depending only on compose.runtime (holdfast-compose/README.md:3-5, build.gradle.kts:30) so it is safe from any UI module — same discipline as the best KMP libraries.

Middleware ordering subtleties (LAST argument is outermost; place logging after validation to observe its errors) are explicitly documented in both KDoc and GUIDE (Store.kt:303-315, GUIDE.md:1239-1242) — the kind of footnote most interceptor APIs make you discover in production.

allFindings.title: Library is not installable: Maven Central badge and install instructions point to artifacts that do not exist
allFindings.evidence: README.md:4 shows a Maven Central badge linking to central.sonatype.com/artifact/com.vynatix/holdfast; README.md:52-68 instructs `mavenCentral()` + `implementation("com.vynatix:holdfast:0.1.0")`. Empirical: `curl https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/vynatix/holdfast/0.1.0/holdfast-0.1.0.pom` returns 404; the whole com.vynatix group is 404 on Central. Additionally, even the local publishing flow is incomplete: ~/.m2/repository/com/vynatix/ contains holdfast, holdfast-coroutines, holdfast-compose but NO holdfast-testing, holdfast-hallmark, or holdfast-hallmark-coroutines — half the advertised module table (README.md:43-50) has never been published anywhere.
allFindings.recommendation: Either publish 0.1.0 to Central before the README advertises it, or replace the badge/install section with explicit 'not yet published — build from source via ./gradlew publishToMavenLocal' instructions including the mavenLocal() repository line. Ensure the publish task covers all six advertised artifacts.

allFindings.title: Advertised testing entry point `holdfastTest { }` does not exist — actual API is `vaultTest(`
allFindings.evidence: README.md:48 and holdfast/README.md:98 advertise '`holdfastTest { }` scope'. The actual public function is `fun vaultTest(` at holdfast-testing/src/commonMain/kotlin/com/vynatix/holdfast/testing/StoreTest.kt:32. Worse, the testing module's own KDocs reference the nonexistent name (StoreHandle.kt:352, matcher/PerformanceMatchers.kt:12,33, concurrency/Eventually.kt:22, concurrency/Awaiting.kt:32, concurrency/Parallel.kt:15). holdfast-testing/ also has NO README.md at all, even though root README.md:48 links to the directory. Three naming generations coexist: vault (vaultTest, `owningVault` in Store.kt:568) → holdfast (docs) → Store (current code).
allFindings.recommendation: Rename `vaultTest` to match the docs (or vice versa — `storeTest` would match the Store rename), sweep all KDoc for vault/holdfast residue, and add a holdfast-testing/README.md with a copy-pasteable test example. The .git-blame-ignore-revs rename machinery exists; finish the rename.

allFindings.title: Forgetting `action` compiles silently and destroys atomicity — invoke-vs-action footgun
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:420 `operator fun <R> invoke(block: Self.() -> R): R` accepts the exact same lambda shape as Store.kt:354 `infix fun <R> action(body: Self.() -> R)`. Store.kt:534-558: `mutate` outside a transaction auto-wraps each write in a one-shot action. Empirically proven in /tmp/holdfast-uxtest: `counter { count update { it + 10 }; label mutate "oops" }` ran with zero warning and produced two separate commits — output showed `observer saw count=11` then `observer saw label=oops` as independent events. A throw between the writes would leave the first committed — exactly the half-updated-state problem the library's pitch (holdfast/README.md:55-58) says it prevents. GUIDE.md §12 Common Pitfalls (lines 995-1003) does not mention this.
allFindings.recommendation: Make multi-mutate-without-action loud: either restrict the invoke operator to subscription-returning blocks (e.g. `subscribe { }` returning Disposable), add a @DslMarker separation, or at minimum add this as the first row of the Common Pitfalls table and a callout in both quick-starts. Consider deprecating bare `invoke` in favor of a named `subscribe`/`with` to break the visual symmetry with `action`.

allFindings.title: Transaction errors are swallowed silently by default; TransactionResult has zero ergonomic helpers
allFindings.evidence: Empirical: the README's own quick-start ends with `counter action { count mutate 99; error("simulated") }` — running it produces NO output, no log, no crash; the Error result is discarded invisibly. Transaction.kt:361-372: `TransactionResult` is a bare sealed interface (Success/Error) with no `getOrThrow()`, `getOrNull()`, `onError {}`, or `fold()` — unlike kotlin.Result which devs expect. GUIDE.md:194 documents 'It never throws — exceptions are captured into Error' but neither quick-start nor Common Pitfalls (GUIDE.md:995-1003) warns that an unexamined result means errors vanish. Coming from MVI/Redux where unhandled exceptions crash or hit an exception handler, this inverts expectations.
allFindings.recommendation: Add kotlin.Result-style extensions (`getOrThrow`, `onError`, `valueOr`) to TransactionResult, and consider an opt-in store-level `onUnhandledError` hook or debug-mode logging when an Error result is created. Document the swallow behavior prominently in both quick-starts.

allFindings.title: Docs claim 'no coroutines dependency in core' — core has an api-scoped coroutines dependency and publicly exposes SharedFlow
allFindings.evidence: holdfast/README.md:12 'No coroutines dependency in core.'; holdfast/README.md:171-173 'no required dependencies beyond kotlin-stdlib + kotlinx-atomicfu'; GUIDE.md:5-6 'no coroutine dependency in its API'. Reality: holdfast/build.gradle.kts:49 `api(libs.kotlinx.coroutines.core)`, and the published holdfast-jvm-0.1.0.module lists kotlinx-coroutines-core in jvmApiElements (verified). Eventful.kt:34 exposes `val events: SharedFlow<E>` in core's public API. Side effect: holdfast-coroutines scopes coroutines as `implementation` (holdfast-coroutines/build.gradle.kts:56) while returning Flow/StateFlow from public functions — that only works because core leaks coroutines api-scoped; if core's scope is ever 'fixed', every holdfast-coroutines consumer breaks at compile.
allFindings.recommendation: Decide the real story: if core needs coroutines (Eventful), update all three doc claims and the module-split rationale; if the goal is a coroutines-free core, move Eventful* into holdfast-coroutines and change holdfast-coroutines's coroutines dep to api() since Flow appears in its public signatures. Right now adopters choosing the library for the claimed zero-coroutines core are being misled.

allFindings.title: Three module READMEs use pre-rename class names that don't exist — samples are not copy-pasteable
allFindings.evidence: holdfast-coroutines/README.md:36 `CounterHoldfast()`, :47 `AccountHoldfast`, :26/:48 variable `holdfast`; holdfast-compose/README.md:23 `CounterHoldfast`, :40 `AccountHoldfast`; holdfast-hallmark-coroutines/README.md:29 `class UserHoldfast`, :3 references a `:validation-coroutines` module that doesn't exist in this repo, and :34-35 calls `holdfast.suspendValidateAndMutate(...)` on a `holdfast` variable that is never defined in the snippet. No class named *Holdfast exists anywhere in the repo (rename commits 539820d/b0c6cb0 changed code but not these docs). A newcomer who lands on a module README after the root README's `CounterStore` quick-start meets a parallel naming universe.
allFindings.recommendation: Mechanical sweep: rename sample classes to CounterStore/AccountStore/UserStore and variables to `store` across all module READMEs; add a CI doc-snippet compile check (e.g. knit or a samples source set) so samples can't rot again.

allFindings.title: Root quick-start is not self-contained: no imports shown, and `effect` is an easy-to-miss top-level import with a cryptic failure mode
allFindings.evidence: README.md:15-39 shows the quick-start with zero import lines and an undefined `handle(result.exception)` placeholder (README.md:31; duplicated at holdfast/README.md:36). Empirical build #1 of the faithful paste: 18 compile errors. The required imports are com.vynatix.holdfast.Store, .TransactionResult, and .effect — the last is a top-level infix function (Effect.kt:26), not a Store member like action/update/mutate, so it's the one you can't guess. Empirical build #4: when the effect import is missing inside a `counter { }` block, the compiler error is NOT 'unresolved effect' at the right place but a cascade starting with "Cannot infer type for type parameter 'R'. Specify it explicitly." pointing at the `counter {` line — actively misleading for a newcomer without an IDE.
allFindings.recommendation: Show the three import lines in the quick-start (standard practice — Orbit and MVIKotlin READMEs show imports or fully-qualified setup), replace `handle(...)` with `println(...)`, and consider making `effect` a member of Store like its siblings so the import asymmetry and the R-inference error cascade disappear.

allFindings.title: Undocumented bleeding-edge toolchain requirements: Kotlin 2.3.21 metadata and JVM target 21
allFindings.evidence: gradle/libs.versions.toml:3 kotlin = "2.3.21", :11 java-target = "21"; holdfast-coroutines/build.gradle.kts:27 `jvmTarget.set(JvmTarget.JVM_21)`. No apiVersion/languageVersion downgrade found in build-logic (grep returned nothing). Neither README.md nor holdfast/README.md states any minimum Kotlin, Gradle, or JDK version. Consumers on Kotlin ≤2.2 toolchains or JDK ≤17 (still the common Android/server baseline) will hit incompatible-metadata or class-file-version 65 errors with no doc to warn them. My scratch project only worked because it pinned kotlin("jvm") 2.3.21 and a JDK 21+.
allFindings.recommendation: Add a 'Requirements' line to the install section (minimum Kotlin X.Y, JDK 21, supported targets: Android/iOS/JVM/wasmJs). Strongly consider setting apiVersion/languageVersion one minor back and jvmTarget 17 for the published artifacts unless 21 is genuinely required.

allFindings.title: holdfast-coroutines README omits suspendAction — the module's headline feature
allFindings.evidence: Root README.md:46 sells the module as '`Flow` / `StateFlow` adapters + `suspendAction { … }` for async transactional bodies'; holdfast/README.md:88 calls suspendAction the first bullet of the module. But holdfast-coroutines/README.md:6-18 'Surface' section lists only asFlow/asStateFlow/first/awaitValue, with no example of suspendAction anywhere in the file. The function exists with an excellent KDoc at SuspendAction.kt:20-58 — I had to read source to write the step-2 sample (which then worked first try).
allFindings.recommendation: Add suspendAction's signature to the Surface block and lift the KDoc example (SuspendAction.kt:48-55) into the README as the first example. Also document the awaitValue signature's actual file location.

allFindings.title: GUIDE.md contains a non-compiling type annotation in the core action example
allFindings.evidence: GUIDE.md:191 `val result: TransactionResult = holdfast action { ... }` — TransactionResult is generic (`sealed interface TransactionResult<out R>`, Transaction.kt:361); a bare generic type in an explicit type position is a compile error ('One type argument expected').
allFindings.recommendation: Change to `val result = holdfast action { ... }` or `val result: TransactionResult<Unit> = ...`. Add doc-snippet compilation to CI.

allFindings.title: Common Pitfalls table cites exception types/messages that don't match the code — undermines error-message searchability
allFindings.evidence: GUIDE.md:1001 cites 'IllegalStateException: Failed to record state change' — that string appears nowhere in src (grep verified); the actual foreign-state message is 'State must be created by this Store instance' (Store.kt:567-568). GUIDE.md:1002 cites 'TransactionException: Cannot mutate state on a Committed transaction' while the mutate path throws IllegalStateException via check() with message 'Cannot mutate state on a ${txn.status} transaction' (Store.kt:547-549). A user pasting the real exception text into the docs/search finds nothing.
allFindings.recommendation: Update the pitfalls table to quote the exact current messages. Also consider enriching the messages themselves with the state's property name and store class (the info exists at the throw site) — 'State must be created by this Store instance' names neither.

allFindings.title: GUIDE.md file-layout and architecture sections are stale
allFindings.evidence: GUIDE.md:111-119 lists `UUID.kt   v4 UUID generator` which does not exist; actual commonMain contains Atomic.kt, Derived.kt, Effect.kt, Eventful.kt, EventfulStore.kt, EventfulSupport.kt, Snapshot.kt, StoreActionDsl.kt, StoreInternalApi.kt — none listed. Stale terminology persists: GUIDE.md:128 '// 1. Define a holdfast.', GUIDE.md:961 'cross-holdfast rejection', GUIDE.md:1001 'foreign-holdfast'; root README.md:45 'cross-holdfast `atomic`'; holdfast/README.md:82,128-137 'cross-holdfast transactions', 'All holdfast writes', 'sorts holdfasts'. After the Store rename, 'holdfast' as a common noun for a store instance forces newcomers to maintain a mental alias table.
allFindings.recommendation: Regenerate the file-layout block from the actual tree, and pick one noun ('store') for instances everywhere, reserving 'Holdfast' strictly as the library brand.

allFindings.title: Compose example's recommended pattern creates name shadowing between the Int snapshot and the State cell
allFindings.evidence: holdfast-compose/README.md:23-31: `val count by holdfast.collectAsState(holdfast.count)` then `holdfast.action { count update { it + 1 } }`. This compiles (lambda-receiver members win over enclosing locals in Kotlin scoping), but the identifier `count` is an Int on line 24 and a State<Int> inside the action lambda — same name, different type, three lines apart, in the canonical example every Compose adopter will copy. Anyone who extracts the action into a non-receiver context (e.g. a helper taking the Int) gets confusing unresolved-reference errors on `update`. The example also uses the stale `CounterHoldfast` type (line 23).
allFindings.recommendation: In the example, name the snapshot differently (`val countValue by ...`) or read `count.value` inside the lambda explicitly; add a sentence explaining which `count` is in scope inside `action { }`. This is the kind of resolution subtlety that should not be load-bearing in a 10-line intro example.

allFindings.title: Multiple subscriptions in one invoke block silently leak all but the last Disposable
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:420 invoke returns only the lambda's last expression. README.md:22 pattern `val sub = counter { count effect { ... } }` works for one effect, but `counter { a effect {..}; b effect {..} }` (which the block syntax visually invites — I wrote exactly this in the probe) returns only b's Disposable; a's subscription becomes uncancellable. No CompositeDisposable/DisposableBag ships in core's Contract.kt surface.
allFindings.recommendation: Provide a `subscriptions { }` builder that collects every Disposable created in the block into one composite Disposable, or document the one-subscription-per-block convention explicitly.

allFindings.title: effect handler uses receiver (`this`) instead of parameter (`it`) — surprising against Flow.collect muscle memory
allFindings.evidence: Effect.kt:26 `infix fun <T : Any> State<T>.effect(handler: T.() -> Unit)`. Every comparable API (Flow.collect, StateFlow collectors, Orbit's intent/reduce) passes the value as `it`. README.md:22's `println("count=$this")` is the only hint; users typing `it` get 'unresolved reference it' and primitives like Int as `this` read oddly (`this + 1`).
allFindings.recommendation: Offer `(T) -> Unit` instead of (or alongside) the receiver form before 1.0 freezes the signature; the receiver form buys nothing for scalar states.

allFindings.title: Action errors vanish silently: result is trivially ignorable and no unwrap affordance exists anywhere
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:354-403 — `action` catches ALL Throwables (including NPE-class bugs) into TransactionResult.Error and 'never throws' (GUIDE.md:201). Transaction.kt:361-371 — the sealed TransactionResult has zero members: no getOrThrow(), valueOrNull(), onError{}, onSuccess{}. Grep across all module API dumps (holdfast, -coroutines, -testing) found no unwrap/assert helper. Kotlin has no unused-result warning, and the infix statement form `store action { ... }` invites discarding the result. Probe (compiled vs holdfast-jvm-0.1.0.jar): a ClassCastException inside an action produced Error(...) and the program continued as if nothing happened. The only error hook, uncaughtObserverHandler (Store.kt:224), covers observers only — action-body exceptions have no default surface (no log, no rethrow).
allFindings.recommendation: Add Result-style members/extensions: `getOrThrow()`, `valueOrNull()`, `exceptionOrNull()`, `onSuccess{}/onError{}` chaining. Add a store-level `unhandledActionError: ((Throwable) -> Unit)?` (or default-rethrow mode) so a discarded Error is never fully invisible. Consider a non-infix `fun <R> runAction(...)` returning R that throws, for users who want exception semantics.

allFindings.title: Self-referential generic is not actually enforced: `class Foo : Store<Bar>()` compiles cleanly, fails at runtime, and the failure is swallowed
allFindings.evidence: Probe compiled `class Foo : Store<Bar>()` against the published jar with ZERO errors/warnings (the recursive bound only requires Bar : Store<Bar>, which holds). At runtime `foo action { ... }` produced `TransactionResult.Error(ClassCastException: class Foo cannot be cast to class Bar)` — via the unchecked `this as Self` at Store.kt:300-301 — meaning a mis-anchored store is a silent no-op if the result is ignored (see blocker above). README.md (intro, ~line 10-13) claims "the type system enforces that a state class anchors itself to its own type" — demonstrably false. By contrast, forgetting the type argument entirely (`class Baz : Store()`) gives a clear compile error.
allFindings.recommendation: Catch the CCE at the `body(self)` boundary and rethrow an enriched IllegalStateException: "Foo must be declared as Store<Foo> (self-type); it was declared as Store<Bar>" — names are available via this::class.simpleName. Correct the README claim (the bound prevents Store<Int>, not Store<SomeOtherStore>). Optionally ship a lint/Detekt rule for `class X : Store<NotX>`.

allFindings.title: Standalone `update` is a non-atomic read-modify-write — loses ~50% of concurrent increments — while StateFlow.update (the audience's reference point) is an atomic CAS loop
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:520-523 — `update` computes `block(this.value)` BEFORE delegating to mutate; outside an action the read is unlocked and only the subsequent mutate gets a one-shot transaction. Runtime probe: 2 threads x 5000 `s { n update { it + 1 } }` produced n=5049 instead of 10000. MutableStateFlow.update {} would give exactly 10000. The KDoc (Store.kt:510-519) and GUIDE.md:1031 say only "equivalent to mutate(block(value))" with no atomicity warning, and GUIDE 7.1 (lines ~440-475) actively recommends the standalone `v { ... }` form for one-liners, claiming "same outcome as action".
allFindings.recommendation: Make standalone `update` wrap the READ in the synthesized action: `if (no owned txn) action { this@update mutate block(this@update.value) }` — the per-store transactionLock then makes it a true atomic RMW matching StateFlow.update semantics. Add an explicit atomicity note to the update KDoc and GUIDE 7.1 either way.

allFindings.title: `store { ... }` (invoke) vs `store action { ... }`: one missing token silently flips atomicity, rollback, and error capture
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:420 — `operator fun invoke` runs the block with no transaction. Runtime probe: `s { a mutate 1; error("boom") }` committed a=1, fired observers, and propagated the exception — whereas the visually near-identical `s action { ... }` would roll back and return Error. Multi-statement invoke blocks compile without complaint; each mutate becomes its own transaction (GUIDE.md:327-329 documents the single-mutate case but never warns about multi-mutate blocks or the mid-block-throw behavior).
allFindings.recommendation: At minimum add a GUIDE/KDoc 'invoke is NOT a transaction' contrast box with the throw example. Stronger: rename the plain context block to something visibly non-transactional (e.g. `with(store) {}` is free from stdlib; or `store.reading { }`), keeping invoke deprecated through 0.x, so the only braces-after-store-name syntax is transactional.

allFindings.title: Lazy state registration makes snapshot()/properties/getState silently incomplete on un-touched stores; restore() failure is then swallowed into the ignorable result
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:432-452 — states materialize only on first delegate READ. Snapshot.kt:31-34 documents that un-touched states are absent ("Touch them explicitly first") — so `snapshot()` on a freshly constructed store returns an EMPTY snapshot, and a persistence flow saves nothing. Worse, restore() into a store whose delegates were never read errors per missing name (Snapshot.kt:67-70) but that error is wrapped in `action` (Snapshot.kt:62) and surfaces only as TransactionResult.Error — silently droppable. getState/hasState/properties (Store.kt:577-586, 204-208) share the same surprise; only getState's KDoc mentions lazy registration.
allFindings.recommendation: Kotlin's `provideDelegate` operator runs at construction: add it to StateDelegate so `by state { }` registers eagerly, eliminating this class of bug with no API change at call sites. If laziness is load-bearing, add `materializeAll()` and make snapshot() call it (or document the trap in snapshot/restore/properties/hasState KDoc uniformly and in GUIDE 14.1).

allFindings.title: distinct=false default inverts the StateFlow contract the target audience carries: same-value commits re-fire observers
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:429-434 — `distinct: Boolean = false`; "every commit fires observers, matching the library's original contract." Runtime probe: 3 commits of the same value fired the effect 4 times (initial + 3); StateFlow/MutableStateFlow always dedup (their core conflation guarantee). Mentioned only in state()'s KDoc and one GUIDE table row (GUIDE.md:1015); README hero example never mentions it. Consequences compound: `derived` backing states are registered without distinct (Derived.kt:64), so derived chains re-fire on no-op recomputes, and UI adapters see redundant fanout.
allFindings.recommendation: Flip the default to `distinct = true` before 1.0 (the 0.x window is the moment), or if the every-commit contract is intentional, rename the parameter to make the choice visible (e.g. `dedupe`) and put a 'differences from StateFlow' callout in README and GUIDE section 2.

allFindings.title: Three names for one concept: store / vault / holdfast — including in permanent public API symbols
allFindings.evidence: Public symbols: `EventfulSupport.bindVault` (EventfulSupport.kt:88, api dump line 43), `MutableState.owningVault` (MutableState.kt:27, api dump line 84 getOwningVault), CoroutineName("VaultProcessScope") (Store.kt:689). User-visible KDoc (IDE quick-doc): "Capability marker for vaults" (Eventful.kt:6), "multiple vaults' transactions" (Atomic.kt:10-17), "singleton vaults" (Store.kt:76), error string "EventfulSupport.bindVault must be called..." (EventfulSupport.kt:90). KDoc examples still subclass as CounterVault/CartVault/MyVault/AccountVault/CredentialsVault (Store.kt:41, Derived.kt:18, EventfulStore.kt:20, EventfulSupport.kt:16, ValidationMiddleware.kt:18, EncryptingTransformer.kt:20). GUIDE.md uses `holdfast` as the receiver variable ("holdfast action {", line 191) and "Cross-holdfast writes" (line 51). A newcomer reading quick-doc must infer vault == holdfast == store.
allFindings.recommendation: Finish the mechanical rename while still 0.x: bindVault→bindStore, owningVault→owningStore, VaultProcessScope→StoreProcessScope, sweep KDoc examples to *Store, replace 'vault(s)' in prose, and pick one generic noun ('store') for GUIDE variable names.

allFindings.title: Genuinely ungated public internals: MutableState constructor, StoreLock, Transaction.commit/rollback are callable from app code without any opt-in
allFindings.evidence: Runtime probe compiled and ran without @OptIn: (1) `MutableState(42, null, store, false)` — constructor is public and unannotated (only the owningVault PROPERTY carries @StoreInternalApi, MutableState.kt:26-28; api dump line 79); (2) `StoreLock().withLock{}` — fully public utility with acquire/release (api dump lines 172-177, StoreLock.kt); (3) `activeTransaction?.commit()` mid-action — Transaction.commit/rollback are public (Transaction.kt:165, 289); subsequent mutate then throws "Cannot mutate state on a Committed transaction" (good guard, but the door shouldn't be open); (4) `properties["a"] as MutableState<Int>` succeeds at runtime despite the KDoc-only "MUST NOT cast" warning (Store.kt:197-203).
allFindings.recommendation: Annotate MutableState's constructor @StoreInternalApi (AnnotationTarget.CONSTRUCTOR is already in the annotation's targets, StoreInternalApi.kt:20). Make StoreLock internal or move it out of the root package behind @StoreInternalApi. Gate Transaction.commit/rollback with @StoreInternalApi (suspendAction already opts in) or document why they are user-callable.

allFindings.title: Middleware ordering (last-registered = outermost) reverses Redux/OkHttp convention
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:303-315 — "the LAST argument is the outermost middleware... Place a logging/audit middleware LAST". Redux applyMiddleware and OkHttp interceptors run first-listed outermost; users porting a Redux mental model will put their logger first and silently miss errors from later-listed middleware. The KDoc is honest and detailed about it, which mitigates — but only for users who read it.
allFindings.recommendation: Either reverse to first=outermost before 1.0, or keep it and add a one-line ASCII ring diagram to the `middlewares(...)` KDoc plus a GUIDE callout titled "ordering is the reverse of Redux".

allFindings.title: MiddlewareContext.metadata is a stringly-typed MutableMap<String, Any> requiring unsafe casts
allFindings.evidence: Middleware.kt:27-31 — `metadata: MutableMap<String, Any>`. Even the bundled TimingMiddleware must cast: `context.metadata[KEY_START_MS] as? Long ?: return` (TimingMiddleware.kt:48), silently skipping on type mismatch. Key collisions between middlewares are possible and unchecked.
allFindings.recommendation: Introduce a typed key (`class MetadataKey<T>(val name: String)` with `operator get/set` on the context) mirroring CoroutineContext.Key; keep the raw map as deprecated escape hatch through 0.x.

allFindings.title: `effect` import friction and receiver-style handler: missing import yields a misleading compile error; `it` is unavailable in handlers
allFindings.evidence: Effect.kt:26 — top-level `infix fun <T> State<T>.effect(handler: T.() -> Unit)`. Probe without the import: errors were "cannot infer type for type parameter 'R'" (on the enclosing store-invoke line) plus "unresolved reference 'effect'" — the inference noise obscures the real fix (add `import com.vynatix.holdfast.effect`). Handler receiver-style means `count effect { println(it) }` does not compile; users must write `this` (README example uses "count=$this"), unlike virtually all observer callbacks in the ecosystem ((T) -> Unit). Also GUIDE.md:325 says "effect is an extension on Store<Self>" — inaccurate; it is a top-level State extension.
allFindings.recommendation: Change handler to `(T) -> Unit` (source-compatible for `this`-free bodies, restores `it`), or add an overload. Fix the GUIDE line. Consider re-exporting effect as a Store member so it resolves inside `store { }` blocks without import.

allFindings.title: Infix `action` cannot carry a transaction name; lambda-derived ids make LoggingMiddleware/TimingMiddleware output near-useless
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:374 — `id = body::class.simpleName ?: Uuid.random().toString()`; for action lambdas this yields synthetic names like `MainKt$increment$1` or random UUIDs. LoggingMiddleware's stated purpose is "transaction's id is included so concurrent traces can be untangled" (LoggingMiddleware.kt:12-13), but no public API lets a user name an action — the infix form has no parameter slot.
allFindings.recommendation: Add a non-infix overload `fun <R> action(name: String, body: Self.() -> R)`. Also expose savepoint info publicly (Transaction.parent is internal — Transaction.kt:22 — yet bundled LoggingMiddleware reads it at LoggingMiddleware.kt:25-26; third-party middleware can't replicate that. Add `val parentId: String?` or `val isSavepoint: Boolean`).

allFindings.title: Store.defaultScope is settable-once-per-process and throws on the second assignment — hostile to test suites
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:711-717 — CAS-guarded setter: second assignment throws IllegalStateException("Store.defaultScope is settable-once"). Any two test classes in the same JVM that both assign it will fail; same for hot-reload/preview environments.
allFindings.recommendation: Provide a @TestOnly reset (wired through holdfast-testing), or make it last-write-wins with a documented race contract like bindToScope already has (Store.kt:91-94).

allFindings.title: 10+ @StoreInternalApi members clutter Store's IDE completion on the primary user-facing class
allFindings.evidence: api dump lines 118-153: alongside ~12 real user APIs, Store exposes lockOrderKey, asyncSerializer (get+set), suspendingOwner (get+set), selfForExternal, internalSetActiveTransaction, internalDrainPostCommitTasks, postCommit, registerInternalState, runUnderLock, snapshotMiddleware. The ERROR-level @RequiresOptIn (StoreInternalApi.kt:13-18) correctly blocks usage, but completion popups on `store.` show them, and `internalSetActiveTransaction` sorts adjacent to legitimate APIs.
allFindings.recommendation: Move companion-module hooks behind a single gated facade (e.g. `@StoreInternalApi val internals: StoreInternals`) so completion shows one gated entry instead of ten. The annotation mechanism itself is right; this is a signal-to-noise fix.

allFindings.title: TimingMiddleware.KEY_START_MS leaks as a public static field despite private companion
allFindings.evidence: api dump line 351: `public static final field KEY_START_MS Ljava/lang/String;` on TimingMiddleware, while the source declares it in a `private companion object` (TimingMiddleware.kt:53-55) — const val JVM lowering bypasses the companion's visibility in the dump.
allFindings.recommendation: Either intentionally publish it (users sharing the metadata key is plausible) and document, or replace `const val` with a non-const internal val to remove it from the ABI.

allFindings.title: Error messages lack identity context
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:176 — every post-dispose call throws bare "store disposed" (no store class name). Store.kt:567-568 — foreign-state mutate throws "State must be created by this Store instance" without naming the property or either store. Compare EventfulSupport.kt:106-114, which names the fix — the library's best messages show the bar the rest should meet.
allFindings.recommendation: Include `this::class.simpleName` in the disposed message and the property name (available via the registry) plus both store classes in the ownership error.

allFindings.title: derived() returns a raw Pair<State<T>, Disposable>
allFindings.evidence: Derived.kt:57-60 — `Pair<State<T>, Disposable>`; call sites destructure positionally (`val (totalState, disposable) = ...`, KDoc example line 49). Pair components carry no names in completion or quick-doc.
allFindings.recommendation: Return a small `DerivedState<T>(val state: State<T>, val subscription: Disposable)` (optionally implementing State<T> by delegation so the handle is directly readable and disposable — matching how Compose's rememberUpdatedState-style handles read).

allFindings.title: GUIDE documents nested-action error semantics that are the opposite of the implementation
allFindings.evidence: holdfast/GUIDE.md:809-821 states 'Inner errors propagate to the outer's catch and roll the outer back' and shows wrapping the inner action in runCatching to recover. But holdfast/src/commonMain/kotlin/com/vynatix/holdfast/Store.kt:384-398 catches every Throwable from the body and returns TransactionResult.Error — an inner `action` NEVER throws, so its error never propagates to the outer and runCatching around it can never catch anything. The library's own test confirms: holdfast/src/commonTest/kotlin/com/vynatix/holdfast/NestedActionTest.kt:89 `nestedActionFailureReturnsErrorWithoutPropagatingToOuterByDefault` (outer SUCCEEDS while the nested action failed). Actual recovery requires `if (nested is TransactionResult.Error) throw nested.exception` (NestedActionTest.kt:129). Real failure mode: an inner action fails, its writes vanish, the outer commits the rest — SILENT partial intent with a Success result on the outer.
allFindings.recommendation: Fix GUIDE 9.8 to match the code: inner action errors are captured into TransactionResult.Error and do NOT abort the outer; show the rethrow idiom (`(inner as? TransactionResult.Error)?.let { throw it.exception }`). Consider adding a `propagate = true` parameter or an `actionOrThrow` variant so composing actions safely is one call, not a manual rethrow ritual.

allFindings.title: TransactionResult.Error is trivially fire-and-forgettable — every runtime guard in the library can be silently discarded
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:354 `infix fun <R> action(body): TransactionResult<R>` — GUIDE.md:201 'It never throws — exceptions are captured into Error.' There is no @CheckResult/@MustUseReturnValue anywhere (grep over all .kt files found none) and no lint guidance. Consequence: the foreign-state ownership error (Store.kt:567-568), Transformer.set validation throws (Store.kt:550 beforeSet inside mutate), restore() missing-state errors (Snapshot.kt:70), and middleware validation failures (ValidationMiddleware.kt:26-28) all funnel into an Error value that the idiomatic call style `fun increment() = action { count update { it + 1 } }` (EventfulStore.kt:23-26 KDoc example) silently drops. Coming from MVI/Orbit where intent handlers either throw or log, this is the most likely 'nothing happened and nothing told me' trap in the library.
allFindings.recommendation: Annotate `action`/`suspendAction`/`restore` with Kotlin 2.2's @MustUseReturnValue (or ship a detekt rule in :holdfast-testing config), and add `Unit`-returning conveniences with explicit semantics: `actionOrThrow {}` (rethrows Error.exception) and/or a store-level `onActionError: ((TransactionResult.Error) -> Unit)?` hook analogous to uncaughtObserverHandler. Document the fire-and-forget hazard in GUIDE §4.2, not just the Success path.

allFindings.title: Observer exceptions during commit fanout are swallowed silently by default; the uncaughtObserverHandler escape hatch is nearly undiscoverable
allFindings.evidence: MutableState.kt:165-176 notifyObservers: `try { observer(value) } catch (e: Throwable) { handler?.invoke(e) }` — with the default `uncaughtObserverHandler = null` (Store.kt:223-224) the exception disappears entirely: no log, no rethrow, no metric. Discoverability: the handler appears ONLY as one row in the GUIDE API reference table (GUIDE.md:1021 'default null = silent swallow'); it is absent from both READMEs, has no narrative GUIDE section, no code sample anywhere, and LoggingMiddleware does not surface observer failures (middleware only sees transaction lifecycle). A dev whose `effect {}` body throws gets a UI that stops updating with zero diagnostics — the classic silent-swallow hazard, verified. Also: if the handler itself throws, it propagates out of notifyObservers into commit and produces a partial commit (see partial-commit finding).
allFindings.recommendation: Make the default handler print to stderr/println with the store class name and a pointer to uncaughtObserverHandler (opt OUT to silence, not opt IN to see), or at minimum add a GUIDE section 'When an effect throws' with a setup snippet, mention it in the README quickstart, and wrap the handler invocation itself in runCatching.

allFindings.title: Exceptions thrown during commit fanout (transformer.get, Bridge.publish, a throwing uncaughtObserverHandler) produce a PARTIAL commit reported as Error
allFindings.evidence: Transaction.kt:241-243 applies pending writes one by one (`pendingWrites.forEach { applyTopLevel(state, value) }`); MutableState.applyCommitted (MutableState.kt:145-149) writes currentValue, then runs afterGet (transformer.get) and `currentBridge?.publish(...)` — both user code that can throw. A throw mid-iteration is caught at Transaction.kt:273-275 → `TransactionException("Commit failed", e)` → Store.kt:390-391 returns TransactionResult.Error. But states applied before the throw KEEP their new committed values with no undo — so the caller holds an Error result while the store is half-mutated, contradicting GUIDE.md:39-40 ('Every transaction is all-or-nothing'). The message 'Commit failed' names neither the state that failed nor which states already applied.
allFindings.recommendation: Either make commit fanout exception-proof (wrap bridge.publish and afterGet per-state in runCatching routed to uncaughtObserverHandler, so commit always completes) or document the partial-commit window explicitly and enrich TransactionException with the failing state's property name and the list of already-applied states.

allFindings.title: suspendAction has no disposed check: on a disposed store it returns Success (no-mutation body) or buried Error instead of throwing like blocking action
allFindings.evidence: Blocking action checks first: Store.kt:355 `checkNotDisposed()` → throws IllegalStateException("store disposed") synchronously (tested in StoreDisposeTest.kt:42-52). But holdfast-coroutines/src/commonMain/kotlin/com/vynatix/holdfast/coroutines/SuspendAction.kt:58-175 never checks isDisposed — it installs the serializer, opens a Transaction via createForExternal, and runs the body. A body that only reads or does I/O returns TransactionResult.Success on a disposed store (silent misbehavior); a body that mutates only fails because mutate's own checkNotDisposed throws inside the body, surfacing as TransactionResult.Error wrapping ISE('store disposed') — easily discarded fire-and-forget. Store.kt:115-118 KDoc even mandates 'Cold APIs in companion modules MUST also check this', a contract :holdfast-coroutines' own entry point violates.
allFindings.recommendation: Add `check(!isDisposed) { ... }` at the top of suspendAction/suspendAtomic so the disposed failure mode matches blocking action (synchronous, loud, before any transaction is created).

allFindings.title: "store disposed" error identifies neither which store nor where it was disposed
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:175-177 `private fun checkNotDisposed() { if (disposedFlag.value) error("store disposed") }` — the entire message is the lowercase string 'store disposed' (also hardcoded at Effect.kt:29). Store has no name and no toString override, dispose() (Store.kt:136) captures no disposal-site breadcrumb, and GUIDE.md contains no occurrence of 'dispose()' lifecycle docs, 'isDisposed', or the error string (grep confirmed) — a dev hitting this in a multi-store app cannot tell which of their stores died or who killed it. Note also state reads are inconsistent post-dispose: registry reads throw, but `state.value` on a retained State reference silently keeps returning the last committed value (MutableState.kt:77-86 has no disposed check).
allFindings.recommendation: Include the concrete class name: `error("${this::class.simpleName} has been disposed; no further reads or mutations are allowed")`, optionally capture a creation/disposal stack in debug builds, and add a GUIDE lifecycle section covering dispose()/isDisposed and the post-dispose behavior of retained State references.

allFindings.title: emit() checks for an active transaction but not for OWNERSHIP — a racy off-action emit silently stages the event onto another thread's transaction
allFindings.evidence: EventfulStore.kt:89-96: `val txn = activeTransaction ?: error("emit(event) called outside of an action / suspendAction. Events must be staged inside a transaction so rollback can discard them.")` — when no action is in flight anywhere, this is the best error message in the library. BUT activeTransaction is a volatile cross-thread read (Store.kt:183-193), and unlike mutate (Store.kt:538 checks `txn.ownerThreadId == currentThreadId()`), emit does no ownership check. If thread B calls store.emit(e) (public API via the Eventful interface) while thread A's action is mid-flight, the event is silently staged onto A's transaction (Transaction.kt:112-119 stagePendingEvent just appends under pendingLock) — it then commits or gets discarded with A's unrelated transaction. Same gap in EventfulSupport.kt:104-116. Timing-dependent: the identical call site throws a clean ISE when no action is running and silently misfiles the event when one is — the worst kind of flaky.
allFindings.recommendation: Mirror mutate's guard in emit: require `txn.ownerThreadId == currentThreadId() || suspendingOwner != null`, else throw the same descriptive 'outside of an action' error. This converts a race-dependent silent misbehavior into the deterministic error users already get in the simple case.

allFindings.title: Foreign-store mutate is caught (good) but the message names neither store nor property, and the GUIDE pitfalls table quotes an error string that does not exist in the codebase
allFindings.evidence: Store.kt:565-570 getMutableState throws IllegalStateException("State must be created by this Store instance") — no property name, no expected-store vs actual-store identification (both are available: ms.owningVault and this@Store). Inside an action this error is additionally swallowed into TransactionResult.Error (see fire-and-forget finding; GUIDE.md:961-971 testing pattern relies on asserting the result). Worse, the Common Pitfalls table at GUIDE.md:1001 tells users to look for 'IllegalStateException: Failed to record state change' — that string appears nowhere in the source (grep confirmed), so a user searching the docs for the REAL message finds nothing and a user reading the docs searches their logs for a message that can never occur.
allFindings.recommendation: Enrich the message: `"State '<name>' belongs to ${ms.owningVault::class.simpleName}, but was mutated through ${this::class.simpleName}. Pass the owning store's state or use atomic(...) for cross-store writes."` (MutableState already knows its owner; thread the property name through from the delegate). Fix GUIDE.md:1001 to quote the actual string.

allFindings.title: restore() onto a freshly-constructed store fails for every never-read property because states register lazily — and the failure is an easily-discarded Error result
allFindings.evidence: Snapshot.kt:62-78: restore resolves each name via getState(name) and errors with 'snapshot contains state '$name' not registered on this store' — a good message in isolation. But states only register on first delegate read (Store.kt:432-452; Snapshot.kt:30-34 documents this for snapshot()), so the canonical persistence round-trip — construct a fresh store at app start, restore a saved snapshot into it — fails for any property not yet touched, even though the property literally exists on the class the user is staring at ('not registered on this store' reads as nonsense to them). And because restore wraps in `action`, nothing throws: it returns TransactionResult<Unit> (Snapshot.kt:55-57), so the idiomatic `store.restore(snapshot)` call silently restores nothing. Misuse case from the brief (snapshot onto a store genuinely missing a property) gets the same buried-Error treatment.
allFindings.recommendation: In restore, fall back to touching/initializing missing states (the store knows its delegates were not read — at minimum say so: '…not registered on this store. Note: states register on first property read; read each property once before restore, or use registerInternalState'). Pair with @MustUseReturnValue on restore so discarding the result warns.

allFindings.title: Exception vocabulary is generic IllegalStateException almost everywhere — programmatic handling requires string matching
allFindings.evidence: The only custom type is TransactionException (Transaction.kt:346-349, used for commit/rollback failure and invalid status transitions). Everything else is bare error()/check() → IllegalStateException: disposed store (Store.kt:176), foreign state (Store.kt:567-568), mutate-on-finalized-txn (Store.kt:547-549 'Cannot mutate state on a Committed transaction'), emit outside action (EventfulStore.kt:91-94), defaultScope re-set (Store.kt:714-716), removeState with pending writes (Store.kt:629), EventfulSupport bind errors (EventfulSupport.kt:89-114), plus IllegalArgumentException in atomic (Atomic.kt:60). Since most of these arrive inside TransactionResult.Error.exception, the natural user code `when (r.exception) { is DisposedStoreException -> retryLater() ... }` is impossible — distinguishing 'store disposed' from 'validation failed' from 'foreign state bug' means parsing message strings, which the GUIDE itself gets wrong (see stale-message finding).
allFindings.recommendation: Introduce a small sealed hierarchy (e.g. HoldfastException: StoreDisposedException, ForeignStateException, EmitOutsideActionException) or at least dedicated subclasses of IllegalStateException for the three errors users will branch on (disposed, foreign-state, outside-action). Keep messages identical to avoid churn.

allFindings.title: No leak detection for undisposed effect{} subscriptions; guidance exists but the only verification tool is locked behind @StoreInternalApi
